prompt: A straight line fitted to complaints coded 0 and 1 predicts −0.21 at 20 minutes. What is wrong?
hint: What range can a probability take?

choices.text: Quick deliveries reduce complaints below zero
choices.why: A probability cannot go below zero, whatever the delivery.

choices.text: Probabilities stay between zero and one
choices.why: Right. A line has no floor or ceiling, and probabilities have both.

choices.text: The coding should have been 1 and 2
choices.why: Any coding gives a line with the same problem.

choices.text: Twenty minutes is outside the data
choices.why: Twenty minutes is in the data; the line fails inside it.

prompt: Of 65 orders that took 50 to 60 minutes, 28 brought a complaint. What share is that, as a percentage? Give one decimal place.
What are the odds of an event with probability 0.8?
Write the odds for an event of probability p.
The model is log-odds = −8.463 + 0.1485 × minutes. At how many minutes is the probability of a complaint exactly one half? Give one decimal place.
hint: A probability of one half is log-odds of zero.

prompt: Why does logistic regression model the log-odds rather than the probability as a straight line?

choices.text: Because log-odds are easier to explain
choices.why: They are harder to explain; that is why odds ratios are used.

choices.text: Because probabilities are always small
choices.why: They can be anywhere from 0 to 1.

choices.text: Because least squares needs logarithms
choices.why: Logistic regression is fitted by maximum likelihood, not least squares.

choices.text: Log-odds have no floor or ceiling
choices.why: Right. Any line converts back to a probability between 0 and 1.

prompt: How are the coefficients of a logistic regression found?

choices.text: By maximum likelihood
choices.why: Right. The coefficients that make the observed outcomes most probable.

choices.text: By least squares on the zeros and ones
choices.why: That is the straight line this lesson set aside.

choices.text: From a closed formula like the slope's
choices.why: There is no closed formula; software improves the answer step by step.

choices.text: By averaging the complaint rate
choices.why: That gives one number, not a curve.

prompt: The coefficient for a first order is 0.8864. What is the odds ratio? Give two decimal places.
hint: e to the power of the coefficient.

prompt: The odds ratio for a first order is 2.43. Which reading is right?
hint: Odds, and what is held fixed.

choices.text: New customers are 2.43 times as likely to complain
choices.why: That would be a ratio of probabilities; at 45 minutes it is 2.08.

choices.text: 2.43% of new customers complain
choices.why: An odds ratio is a multiplier, not a share.

choices.text: Their odds are 2.43 times, at equal minutes
choices.why: Right. Odds, not probability, and with delivery time held fixed.

choices.text: First orders cause 2.43 more complaints
choices.why: It is a ratio, and the data cannot show a cause.

prompt: At 60 minutes, the same odds ratio of 2.43 gives a ratio of probabilities of only 1.36. Why?
hint: How much room is left above 0.75?

choices.text: The model changes at 60 minutes
choices.why: It is one model; its scale is the reason.

choices.text: First orders matter less when slow
choices.why: On the log-odds scale they matter exactly as much.

choices.text: Near 1, a probability has little room left
choices.why: Right. Near 1, probabilities cannot grow much, while odds still can.

choices.text: The confidence interval is wider there
choices.why: That concerns uncertainty, not the ratio itself.

prompt: A cut-off of 0.5 catches 81 of the 114 real complaints. What is the sensitivity, as a percentage? Give one decimal place.
At a cut-off of 0.2, 166 calls are made and 100 reach a real complaint. What is the precision, as a percentage? Give one decimal place.
Predicting no complaint for every order scores 71.5% accuracy. What does that show?
hint: How many complaints does that rule catch?

choices.text: Accuracy rewards the common outcome
choices.why: Right. Sensitivity, 0% here, shows the rule is useless.

choices.text: The logistic model is barely better
choices.why: The model catches most complaints; the empty rule catches none.

choices.text: Complaints are too rare to model
choices.why: Over a quarter of orders complained; they are not rare.

choices.text: The cut-off should be 0.715
choices.why: The 71.5% is a share of orders, not a probability cut-off.

prompt: A missed complaint loses a customer; an unnecessary call costs a minute. Which cut-off suits Horta better?

choices.text: The higher one, since it is more accurate
choices.why: Accuracy weighs both mistakes equally; here they cost very differently.

choices.text: Always 0.5, the standard
choices.why: No cut-off is standard; costs decide it.

choices.text: Whichever gives the best precision
choices.why: Precision ignores the complaints that are missed.

choices.text: The lower one, since false alarms are cheap
choices.why: Right. It catches more complaints, and false alarms are cheap.

prompt: Match each outcome to the model that fits it.
hint: Number, yes or no, count, time.

prompt: Which goal favours interpretable coefficients and attention to confounders?
hint: What does the question ask: why, or what next?

choices.text: Predicting new cases as well as possible
choices.why: Prediction cares most about error on new data.

choices.text: Explaining how one thing affects another
choices.why: Right. The coefficient is the answer, so it has to mean something.

choices.text: Maximising accuracy
choices.why: That is a prediction goal, and it can mislead.

choices.text: Fitting the training data closely
choices.why: That is the road to overfitting.

prompt: Why do the residuals of a straight line fitted to zeros and ones break lesson 20's assumptions?
hint: What values can a residual take when y is 0 or 1?

choices.text: They add up to more than zero
choices.why: Least-squares residuals add up to zero here too.

choices.text: Two values each, with uneven spread
choices.why: Right. Not normal, and widest near a probability of 0.5.

choices.text: There are too few of them
choices.why: There are 400; the problem is their shape.

choices.text: They depend on the order of the deliveries
choices.why: Nothing here is collected in a time order that matters.

prompt: What do linear, logistic and Poisson regression have in common?
hint: A straight line, linked to the outcome.

choices.text: They are all fitted by least squares
choices.why: Logistic and Poisson use maximum likelihood.

choices.text: They need a binary outcome
choices.why: Only logistic regression does.

choices.text: They give probabilities as output
choices.why: Linear regression gives a number, Poisson an expected count.

choices.text: A line in the predictors, on a suited scale
choices.why: Right. They are all generalised linear models.
